Journals is the engine and Notes owns the page; Journals owns the engine that turns sources into sections, the agenda, snapshots, reviews and the journal views, and never the pages row, one journal per date, the /summary block interface or the free-form entry.
Each module computes its metrics and Journals presents them; Journals never re-implements metric math, it schedules and personalizes the presentation.
In the app the journal registry holds every built module contribution; the composition root calls each module's journal registration helper, and Journals itself names none.

The journal of the day, in Notes and on Home, is composed of each module's own blocks (capability-registry entries with an inline target, shown as checklists, lists, number cards or graphs), switched on per module by the journal's toggles; there is no single aggregated summary block, and each block reads its module's day live through its journal contribution, so a change in the module shows in the journal.

The journal types and the selection logic have one home, the core Journals module; the web layer re-imports them and its inert copies (the signature-only contribution registry and the selection storage seams) are retired.
Preferences stores the global default journal selection, which modules' blocks show, and in which form, when a journal has no override (JR-4's default half).
A snapshot's frozen section data is encrypted client-side [E]; the snapshot date and capture time are plaintext. M1 is a pass-through.

Each past day is captured as a snapshot by a defined trigger, against a strict local-time today; snapshots stay immutable and freeze degraded sections as they are, and whether a backfill after capture re-captures the day is a design pass.
The user plans when each review arrives, and the scheduled review is delivered through a scheduled item, a Sessions planned item or a Notifications delivery.
The journal of the day renders its terminal states, loading, first day with each module block's own nothing-yet, a failed contribution degrading only its block, and populated; it is never blank.
The data-model record shows the journal_snapshots table and the generalized summary_config selection.
The engine sits above the modules; Journals depends downward on the modules and on Notes, and Notes, a foundation, never depends on Journals.

The user works from the journal; a module block is interactive (tick a task, check a habit, start a session) and writes only through its module's own service, so the journal is the one place to see and act on the day without going to each module.
Modules contribute through a registry and the journal names no module; each module registers a journal contribution, and the engine iterates the registry, so adding a module never edits the journal.

The user picks, per module, which of the module's blocks the journal shows and in which form, with each contribution advertising what it offers; a per-journal override in summary_config, generalized from the five fixed toggles to a per-module selection, wins over the global default.
The journal of the day has two halves, the summary (what happened) and the agenda (what's due); the agenda reads the shared Sessions due agenda that also feeds Sessions and the Global Calendar.
Today's journal is live and re-aggregates on open; a past day shows the snapshot of that day, with an optional live then-vs-now comparison the user opts into.
A summary contribution answers for a given date deterministically, from data keyed to that date, so a snapshot is a faithful record of the day.

Reviews compose snapshots over time-frames the user defines (day, week, month, year and custom ones such as bi-week, bimester or semester), arrive when the user schedules them, and render in a dedicated Wrapped-style view; a period with too little history is an explicit not-enough-data state.
A review shows improvement as a trajectory, progress against goals, dreams and purposes, how projects developed, and the workload and output in the period, never a list.

Knowledge content is encrypted (an object's title, description and key concepts, a reference's title, source and link, a compound set's spec, a lab entry's hypothesis and conclusion, a card's front, back, hint and explanation); kinds, realms, enums, dates, counters, mastery numbers and sort orders stay plaintext.

Knowledge mastery is an Education measurement source; Knowledge exposes a subject's mastery compounded from object mastery, assessment results and pace against the syllabus, Education owns the program rollup, and Knowledge never writes Education's measurement.

A compound set (one consumer module's partition with the user's rules, methods and parameters) is built in a builder, and a default set ships so no user is forced to personalize; a model may help build one only by opt-in and consent.
Nothing publishes from within Vida and there is no community surface; a setup is reproduced by following its steps, never shared as an object.

The Knowledge Lab turns a hypothesis and live data from the user's own modules into a conclusion that can be promoted into a catalog object, and a lab entry is a link target, so a research deliverable can point at it.
References are first-class (a title, a source, a link and a type, scoped to an object), replacing the old array of links.

Knowledge emits after the write, failure-isolated and dormant without a handler; a recorded review emits award_xp and emit_measurement_signal once per review event, a review with a quality also emits mastery changed, and an object created or a lab concluded reaches the journal by pull only.
Knowledge's journal contribution answers a date with the objects added and the reviews recorded that day, empty on an idle day, and is registered through registerKnowledgeJournal.

Knowledge has its own blocks (capability entries with an inline target), such as what's due to study today with a start action, the day's reviews and mastery by area; each reads Knowledge live and writes only through its service, separate from its journal contribution.
Knowledge serves a read provider for knowledge objects, containers and cards in the shared view registry, so views, sessions and blocks that target them resolve instead of degrading.

Knowledge registers a due lane that serves the objects due for review on the Sessions due agenda, each keyed by its subject (knowledge_object and the object id), so the Calendar, the journal and Notifications read them and the study push toggle gates a reminder.
A knowledge object is never the same row as an Education planning topic; the two are separate entities, linked, and deleting the Education topic never deletes the acquired knowledge.

In the app the composition root builds the capability registry, the review engine, Knowledge (with spaces, backlinks, notes and the effects rail and its shared registry) and Flashcards (with sessions and the session registry), and registers Knowledge's journal contribution, due lane and read provider and Flashcards' method and sub_type; Knowledge owns no effect handler.

Knowledge serves its measures as measurement sources per entity (mastery per object, the reviews recorded, the due backlog), so Purposes' bindings, the user's own measures and Gamification's rules can read them, including no study by a deadline or in a period.

Every study is a session; studying an object, a drill included, runs through Sessions, the user can name it and choose its type (study or review by default), it attaches to what it covers, and each outcome records a review on that session.

Knowledge ships opt-in datasets the user accepts or declines (curve and method presets, starter kind trees, each consumer's default compound set, curated reference objects and starter decks), refreshed as a whole set and read from a local copy, filling objects and cards in one step; hand authoring always stays.
Knowledge is searchable through a full-text index over object and note text, and until the index exists the search answers search-unavailable, never an empty list.
Objects can be auto-populated from a syllabus, a table of contents or a schedule, opt-in and on the device, and a refused or unavailable source is reported, never a silent no-op.
A model may suggest a compound set only on the user's request and consent; Knowledge never applies a suggestion itself or holds a model key, and an unavailable or denied model reads as unavailable.

Knowledge's surfaces (the all-knowledge page, per-object pages and the graph) ship a working default (a default kind tree and one starter container), show empty, loading, error and populated states, and regroup containers per view.
A topic links to its assessments once Education has them, instead of carrying an exam flag.
Knowledge raises typed errors only, a failed write reverts, a broken kind or parent reference is rejected at write, and a mismatch across modules is flagged, never guessed.

Knowledge lives on the Subject, Unit, Topic spine, and below a topic the user grows their own hierarchy of objects through parent_object_id; every object has a kind from a user-extensible registry, with topic, concept and definition shipped as editable, removable defaults.
The user sees their progress per area and per Vida module; an area's progress reads its member subjects' mastery live, never a stored copy.

Every kind declares a learning realm (understand, memorize or the user's own), and the realm picks the default study method, memorize toward drills and understand toward elaboration, always overridable by the user.
A knowledge note is a pages row with a knowledge entity type and a personalizable render, never a knowledge_notes table and never an inline column.
Objects reach courses, books, skills, languages, finance and health through entity links, many per object, never a resource_type check.
Containers organize as Module, Area and Subject with many-to-many membership at every step through scoped tags, never one parent chain, and an area can serve several Vida modules.

Study methods (flashcards, Feynman, self-test and more) and review curves are user-selectable and mixable per area, subject, unit, topic or kind, and `SM-2` is one preset in the scheduling family, never the model.
Mastery is derived at the leaf from whichever active methods report under the object's chosen curve and rolls up kind, topic, unit and subject; the user tunes the curve, never the number.

Four measurement kinds normalize to 0 to 1; quantitative is a direction-aware clamp over current, baseline and target, milestone is done or n of m, rate is a clamped ratio, and qualitative is the rating over its scale.
A source outage reads the last-known value with a flag, never null as if fresh and never a fabricated number, and raises the typed SourceUnavailable.
Bindings live in one shared table of source, target and mode for every module, which the acyclic guard reads; no module stores a binding reference in its own columns.

In the app the composition root builds one shared measurement source registry, passes it to every module that reads it (Purposes, Projects) and lets each composed module advertise its sources into it.
The engine adds non-linear progress curves and a size limit for the binding graph, so a large graph stays fast and a curve shapes a measure without changing its stored value.
Multi-condition and user-authored automation over measures rides the economy's rules and the capability-authoring rail, never a second automation engine in the measurement substrate.

The user personalizes measurement with their own parameters; they can override how a goal computes onto measurements and bindings, make one measure count for more than one goal or meaning, map a qualitative ladder to values, pick a progress curve, and add a plugin measurement kind when the four don't fit.
A qualitative measure with no scale or no rating is null (unmeasured), never 0.

The rollup is the sum of child progress times weight over the sum of weights; a null or 0 weight counts as equal weight, unmeasured children are excluded, and an empty or all-unmeasured set is null, never 0.
Progress derives on read; a stored value is an override, null means derive, and it is never a stored counter.
A binding mode is manual, derived-pull or event-trigger, and an event-trigger fires an existing rail effect, never a new engine.

A module advertises a queryable measure in the measurement source registry and a consumer queries it, never a table read; an unadvertised key reads null, never a fabricated value, and real sources are each module's own.
The acyclic guard rejects a binding cycle over both edge modes with a typed error; the binding edge type is shared contract, and the economy's rule edges reuse it.
A pursuable declares its measurement_kind and computes its own progress; the substrate owns the contract, and Purposes consumes it.

A measurement source registers per entity type and answers asynchronously for one entity, optionally for a named measure over a range of days, day by day; a stored type:id reference still resolves, so a derived-pull binding (PG-6, PG-15) reads the measures Projects, Books, Check-ins, Habits, Health and Finance advertise.
Notifications reads every module through seams and writes only its own rows; nothing in Vida depends on it, so it can be switched off and no core function breaks.

A notification points at its subject through entity_type, entity_id and a deep-link action_url and never copies the subject's data beyond the title and message the producer supplied; a deleted subject leaves the row readable.

The title, message, action label and metadata are encrypted; the type, the subject link, the action link, the read and archive flags, the timestamps, the delivery audit and the effect key stay plaintext.
The type is one of info, success, warning, error, reminder and achievement, fixed for v1; every documented producer maps onto them and no type is added.
A notification is marked read on view, archived on dismiss, auto-archived once expired and purged after a long time archived; the unread badge derives from live rows.
Achievement and level-up notifications come from Gamification through surface_notification; Notifications records and delivers them and never evaluates an achievement.
Grouping reminders into a daily or weekly digest through the Preferences notification_frequency is target vision; v1 delivers each notification in real time.

In the app the composition root builds Notifications with the delivery engine, the Sessions due agenda and a Preferences port, registers its surface_notification handler into the one shared effect registry before any write can emit, registers its journal contribution, and runs an on-device loop that ticks the dispatcher and the expire and purge sweeps.

Notifications' journal contribution answers a date with the unread badge by attention type (unread, alerts, warnings, reminders), empty when nothing is unread, and is registered through registerNotificationsJournal.

Notifications has its own journal blocks, such as the day's alerts and the reminders that fired; each reads Notifications live and acts only through its service (mark read, archive), separate from its journal contribution.
Notifications serves a notification read provider in the one shared view registry, so a view or a block lists notifications without reading the table.

A notification comes either from the surface_notification effect (a thing happened) or from the dispatcher firing a due reminder read from the Sessions due agenda (a thing is due); both land as one row shape in one stream, and no module writes the table directly.
A due reminder converges to one row across devices; the time row carries a deterministic occurrence key (source, subject, deadline) that sync resolves like the event key.

The inbox reads live through the Notifications service, its read and archive actions persist, it shows each capability's loading, empty, error and success states, and a link to a deleted subject resolves to a calm "no longer available" state.

The surface_notification payload is the fire input (one of the six types, a non-empty title, and optional message, action, subject link, expiry and metadata); Notifications exports its schema so a producer validates before it emits and a rule's consequence is checked when saved, and the handler still skips a bad payload without throwing but flags it.
The dispatcher reads the user's refuse-every-third-party choice from Preferences at each delivery and runs the engine in that mode, so only in-app and native local alerts are used.

The data-model record shows the notifications delivery audit (delivered in-app, push and email), the encrypted metadata, the nullable effect_event_id with its `UNIQUE` constraint and the read, archive and expiry lifecycle.
Upcoming reminders are derived from the due agenda and never stored; a row materializes only when a reminder actually fires, so the table is the history of what already fired.
Channels, quiet hours and the per-module push toggles belong to Preferences; Notifications reads them at each delivery and stores none of them, and with no Preferences port every channel is on.

Before delivering, the dispatcher checks the channel, the per-module toggle and quiet hours; a suppressed notification is still recorded in-app, so suppression means not pushed or emailed, never lost.

Push is a content-free wake signal and the device composes the notification after it syncs and decrypts; the server never sees a title, message or subject link, email is a generic nudge only and there is no `sms`.
In-app is the always-available local channel; it has no zero-knowledge limit and is never gated away, only the external channels can be off.
An event notification converges to one row by its deterministic effect_event_id, and a due reminder is keyed by its due occurrence, so a retry or two devices waking fire it once.
A fire succeeds on the device first, and the row with its read and archive state syncs to the other devices, so reading it on one clears it on the rest.
No inline notes columns, ever; every note for any entity is a pages row addressed by entity_type and entity_id.
Every page type is editor-capable; the page surface gates on page type, never on the ENTITY_TYPES registry.
A rename is a metadata edit through updatePage; links are unaffected, with no optimistic patching.
Page templates are live layouts; applying forks a saved layout into a new page, and capture takes authored structure only, never accumulated data.

Notes stores summary_config only, the journal's per-module toggles; the journal page holds each module's own blocks, switched on by those toggles and read live through the Journals contributions, never one summary block; each block degrades alone, and the full personalizable menu of module blocks is intended (G5).

Inline blocks are ADR-008 capability-registry entries; the palette offers the page's Spaces' capabilities plus the editor base, /summary, /entity-link and /backlink get bodies, and the rest stay honest placeholders.
The [[ candidates are every OS entity that is a page, binding page_links for a page and entity_links for an entity; hovering a link shows a title and type preview card.
A page's attachments upload as a blob with a lazy thumbnail, and the page lists its live attachments.
The /notes collection lists note pages that are not archived, in List, Gallery and Neural layouts; layout, filter and sort persist in a global ADR-007 views row, and tags filter the list.
Card data is derived client-side; the excerpt comes from the decrypted content, the row date is journal_date or else the local day of updated_at, and word_count is derived.
The /pomodoro block launches a Sessions focus timer and the page links to that session.
One journal per calendar date among live rows, the user's local day; a second one is a typed JournalExistsError, never an overwrite.
Each page type has its own Overview; note shows properties, attachments and backlinks, journal is the daily dashboard the Journals module owns, and merged mode renders the same sections as one page.
The task_note and task_group_note Overviews ride fe-tasks through the Overview registry.
The milestone_note and deliverable_note Overviews ride fe-projects through the Overview registry.
Merged or tabbed mode is remembered per page on this device in app_state, with per-type defaults; a mere open never writes.
Favorite and archive are booleans, the icon is a Lucide name, and the cover is an http(s) image URL or one of the page's attachments.
Full-text search is FTS5 over decrypted content, rebuilt on unlock, with no plaintext mirror; until indexed the surface says search is unavailable.
Backlinks merge page links and entity links grouped by source module, and the neural graph renders the link graph, honestly empty while its data prep is deferred.

Trash is one system surface for every module, listed in the System panel and grouped by module; a cross-module provider registry (listDeleted, restore, purge) feeds it, notes registering first, and restore, delete forever and Empty Trash sit behind danger confirms.
Each content write reconciles the page's page_links and entity_links rows to the wiki-links in its document, with set semantics.
Page title, content, cover and summary_config, link context and attachment files and thumbnails are encrypted client-side [E]; M1 is a pass-through.
Editor content has its own write path (writePageContent), never the LWW metadata patch, and merges as a per-page Yjs CRDT at sync (M4).
Page links and entity links are unique and id-based; re-linking is an idempotent no-op or a revive.
Entity links and entity notes target a registered type in the open ADR-006 registry, validated in-service (UnregisteredEntityTypeError).
Wiki-links resolve by page id, never by text or slug; the [[ picker binds a concrete target_page_id, so links survive renames and title clashes.
Entity notes auto-exist with their parent entity and are never blank, seeded deterministically client-side from the parent's fields.

A user delete is a soft delete with undo, and the page waits 30 days in the one Trash all modules share (NP-27); hard delete is an explicit confirm and an app-layer cascade, since there are no SQL foreign keys.
A pomodoro is always the runtime of a focus session and attaches to a session_id, never to a task, note or class; starting a timer is starting or resuming a focus session.

A completed focus session fires its declared award_xp effect (granted as grant_currency into the consequence_ledger) and surface_journal (the daily focus feed), with no bespoke Pomodoro wiring to Gamification or Journals.
Focus analytics (completed count, focus time, planned-vs-actual, focus streaks) are a derived cut of the session log, never a synced Pomodoro aggregate.

A pomodoro's effects are scoped to its session's attachments, never count one event twice, need opt-in consent for sensitive modules, and a failed effect is typed and logged while the completion still records.
Focus Mode is the runtime's low-distraction face; it composes the session type's declared tools per sub_type and per platform (mobile, desktop, web), and is never hard-wired to one module.
A config change during a run applies to the next interval and never edits the running one.
Starting focus without a session_id first creates a focus session carrying the caller's attachment, and a failed creation is a typed NoFocusSession, never a timer with no session.
Only interval boundaries persist (start, pause, complete, accumulated pause and interruption); the per-second countdown is client state, never written per tick.
A completed focus session declares surface_journal, a projection with no handler that feeds the daily focus feed; this is the Sessions half of PD-10, whose award_xp half is Gamification's.

Completing focus closes its session through the one firing path, and cancelling it closes the session as skipped with no effects; a focus run's state changes only through startFocus, pauseFocus, completeFocus and cancelFocus.
The /pomodoro widget is a view, never an owner; in a page it lists the focus sessions, launches one and links the page's analytics to that session.
Interval durations are Preferences-owned and the runtime only obeys them; named focus templates are focus-session presets owned by Sessions, with at most one default.

Interval type (focus, short_break, long_break) and status (running, paused, completed, cancelled) are fixed enums mirrored by a database constraint, and a long break follows every sessions_before_long focus intervals.
Paused time is excluded from focus; real focus is elapsed minus total paused time.
Cancelling mid-focus records was_interrupted and an optional reason, which feed focus analytics.
Auto-start of breaks and of the next interval, notifications and sounds govern interval boundaries, each with a sane default and user-overridable.
A break carries per-session-type guidance in Focus Mode (hydrate, recompose, rest, a suggested activity), not a bare countdown.
Time to a task flows only through the focus session's log_time effect into task_time_logs; Pomodoro never writes actual_minutes.

Values' names and descriptions, purposes' titles, descriptions, visions and whys, targets' titles, descriptions, units and success criteria, metric names, descriptions and units, metric context notes, review reflections and notes, contribution notes, plan step titles and notes, and dreams' titles, descriptions and estimated cost are encrypted client-side [E]; enums, dates, numeric measures and references stay plaintext. M1 is a pass-through.

A contribution is a first-class weighted edge from a habit, routine, project, task, dream, finance target or check-in into a purpose or target, holding only the weight and notes, never a copied value; it is Purposes' own mechanism, not a shared association primitive.

A goal decomposes into action through Tasks and Projects, milestones and deliverables; plan steps are an ordered, checkable documentation layer on a task or target, and a step that needs real tracking graduates into a sub-task, never a parallel registry.
Target reviews (a progress rating, a reflection and next actions) and purpose reviews (alignment and fulfillment) are two distinct shapes, never merged.

A due purpose or target review is a review session surfaced through the due agenda to the Global Calendar, the journal agenda and Notifications, never a Purposes reminder; it shares the scheduling seam with Check-ins reviews but not their content.

Purposes registers as a provider, a day summary of goals, targets, reviews due and progress deltas for the journal and a due lane of review dates for the Calendar and the agenda; the aggregators iterate their registries, and neither side names the other.

A quantitative metric may derive-pull its value from a module that advertises a queryable measure, through the measurement source read seam and never a table read; a metric value keeps a manual or auto provenance, and metrics carry their direction and baseline.
Dreams are the single aspiration entity and absorb the retired bucket list items; the Bucket List is a Space over dreams (a tag and a gallery view), not a module.
Progress, contribution rollups and alignment trends recompute from current state and the review and metric ledgers; no stored progress or streak counter is trusted, override slots excepted.

Values, purposes, targets and dreams get standalone pages, tags come from the Spaces vocabulary and links from entity_links, all written through the Spaces and Notes services; a metric value is a tag and link target only, and no inline notes column exists.

Deleting a purpose clears its targets' purpose (they survive standalone) and a value clears its purposes' value; contributions, reviews and metric values go with their owner, and soft delete hides while keeping history.

Nothing in Vida requires a purpose and anything may ladder into one; Purposes is the meaning plane (where life is going), a separate axis from the journal's operational plane (what happened and what is due), never merged with it.
Every create, edit, measure, review and bind succeeds locally first; structured columns sync last-writer-wins and the ledgers merge by natural key.

Purposes' journal contribution answers a date with the active purposes and the targets whose review is due, empty on an idle day; the root composes Purposes, so registering it is one call that nobody makes yet.

Purposes has its own blocks (capability entries with an inline target), such as goal progress, reviews due and the values ladder; each reads Purposes live and writes only through the Purposes service, so the journal and any page can show and work on them.

Purposes has standalone pages for values, purposes, targets and dreams with derived progress, contributors and reviews, a values layer, a view of the life domains, and the Bucket List vision board as a gallery over dreams.

Each Purposes capability renders its terminal states (loading, empty with a call to action, a typed error with retry, success); an unmeasured goal shows unmeasured, never 0 percent, and a failed source read shows a flagged partial.

Purposes feeds the Sessions due agenda with target reviews (built), purpose reviews and the deadlines of targets, purposes and dreams, so the Global Calendar and the journal agenda show them without copying them.
Purposes serves a ReadProvider for purposes, targets, values and dreams into the shared view registry, so saved views and other modules list and title them.
Preferences gates review reminders with their own push toggle, keyed so the toggle matches the purposes due rows; there is no Purposes toggle today, so only the global push switch governs them.

Completing a purpose or target emits emit_measurement_signal only, once per transition into completed, after the write, failure-isolated and dormant without a handler; Purposes grants no points, and Gamification's rule turns the signal into a reward.

Every pursuable exposes progress from 0 to 1 through its measurement_kind (quantitative with direction and baseline, milestone or checklist, rate, qualitative by a self-rating scale or a status ladder); an abstract goal is measured by judgment, never left untracked, and reference data contributes no progress.
A review check-in records target reviews through Purposes, the same openTargetReview path, so the review lands in the target's ledger and reschedules its next review.

In the app the composition root builds Purposes with the Tasks, Habits, Routines, Projects, Check-ins, Finance and Education services it reads (PG-37), the shared measurement source registry for its bindings (PG-6, PG-15) and the effects rail with its registry, next to its sessions, spaces and notes, and registers its due lane (built), its journal contribution (PG-21) and its read provider (PG-26).
Reviewing a goal is a session the user can name and type (review by default), attached to the target or purpose it reviews, and completing it records the review; the review sub_type has one owner.
Deleting a contributor in its own module removes its contributions, so the goal's rollup re-derives and its contributor list never shows a deleted entity.

The data-model record shows the ten built Purposes tables (values, purposes, targets, metrics, metric values, target and purpose reviews, contributions, plan steps, dreams), no junctions and no foreign keys, targets with measurement_kind and an optional purpose, and no bucket list table.

Status, priority, life domain, review frequency, calculation method, metric source, contribution goal and contributor types, plan step owner type and dream category and status are closed enums declared once (string unions, `CHECK` constraints and `Zod` schemas).

Purposes takes the services of the modules that can relate to a goal (Tasks, Habits, Routines, Projects, Check-ins, Finance, Education) as deps, like Routines, and reads each related entity's day through them, done or not done and its own figure or progress, reflection only and never a write; it computes that day's progress for each purpose, goal and dream, keeps no copy, nothing is pushed to it, and it never reads the journal or, by default, the measurement engine or registry; the user can override a goal to compute through measurements (MS-15).
A value's progress rolls up its purposes, and a dream derives its progress from its steps or its project when no override is set, so every spine entity measures.

An Education subject, grade or assessment, and its components, can relate to a purpose, goal or dream as a contributor; Purposes reads them through the Education service like its other contributors, and grades and their averages stay Education's own computation.
A measurable derives its value from its kind and sources by default; the stored progress and current value columns are override slots, null means derive, and they are never the source of truth.

Progress rolls down from children and up from contributor to target to purpose by the same weighted normalization, the sum of progress times weight over the sum of weights, so heterogeneous kinds compose into one goal.

A measurable declares how it is fed, manual, derived-pull (computed from a linked entity's source on read) or event-trigger (set when a linked entity changes state); auto-sourced metrics and auto-completing tasks are the same primitive, distinct from a value's provenance source.

An event-trigger write goes through the owning module's single service method on the effect rail, idempotent per effect_event_id, never a new engine; writes are sparse, and rollups and what changed derive on read from each related entity's day (PG-37).
Bindings form an acyclic graph; a binding that would close a cycle, made directly or by an edit, is rejected at author time with a typed error and not saved.
The spine is values above purposes above targets, with dreams beside them, and every joint is optional, so a standalone value, purpose, target or dream is valid.

A project's title, description and vision, a milestone's and a deliverable's title and description, a document's name and file, and the tag associations are encrypted client-side [E]; scope, complexity, status, priority, dates, progress, color and icon are plaintext config. M1 is a pass-through.

Projects links to other modules only through junctions and documented integration points; project_habits stays (Habits), purpose_projects is retired into the weighted contributions (Purposes), a dream keeps its project link, and Projects owns project contacts with roles, project to account links and project events.

Third-party metric ingestion for a deliverable is opt-in and device-mediated under an external-in grant, never a server-side fetch; an ingestion that would need the server to see plaintext is refused with a typed consent error unless the user opted in.
Projects, milestones and deliverables are tagged through the shared scoped entity_tags, never an inline tag list; every write succeeds locally first and structured columns sync last-writer-wins.

A task can sit under a deliverable (which implies its milestone and project), and a deliverable's task leaf counts only the tasks nested in it, never the milestone's tasks outside it (Victor, 2026-11-08).

Deleting a project, a milestone or a deliverable asks the user what happens to its tasks (delete, unlink or move them) and calls the Tasks operations for the choice; Projects never leaves a task pointing at a deleted parent.

Project time also counts sessions attached to the project, one of its milestones or one of its deliverables, derived on read from the session log and counted once per session; a time log on a project target still writes nothing.

An agent over the vault runs on-device or in the cloud as the user picks per use, acts only within its granted envelope through a mediated model call, marks what it writes with source ai, and never sends vault plaintext to the cloud without the user's opt-in.
Listing projects filters by status and scope and hides soft-deleted rows; archived is a status filter (completed or cancelled), not a separate state.

Scope, complexity, status and priority are closed enums declared once (string unions, `CHECK` constraints and `Zod` schemas), progress is 0 to 100 or empty, and estimated and actual hours are stored as minutes despite the name.

The user picks how to see projects; the Projects Dashboard, the Projects Timeline, a pinned project, and the project, milestone, deliverable and project task standalone pages, each in a layout the user chooses (timeline, board, Kanban or archived), with reads and optimistic writes refreshed up the hierarchy.

A project has four levels, Project > Milestone > Deliverable > Task; a milestone belongs to one project and nests under a milestone of the same project with no cycle, a deliverable sits under exactly one milestone, and a task sits under the project, a milestone or a deliverable through the Tasks parent links (the deliverable link is PJ-13; every milestone has a deliverable, PJ-35).

Each Projects capability renders its terminal states (loading, empty with a call to action, a typed error with retry, populated); a measured deliverable whose source fails shows a flag and its last-known value, and a rollup over a partial read is flagged.
A project page is a hub; it shows the project's habits, the purposes it contributes to, its dreams, accounts, contacts, events and check-in reviews, each read through its owning module's service.

A research or investigation is an artifact deliverable (milestone kind, manual binding) linked to a Knowledge Lab entry; Projects tracks the deliverable, Knowledge holds the exploration, and there is no investigations table.

Completing a project or a milestone emits emit_measurement_signal only, once, after the write, failure-isolated and dormant without a handler; Projects grants no points itself, and Gamification's rule turns the signal into points.

Projects' journal contribution answers a date with the active projects and the milestones due that day, empty on an idle day; it is registered into the journal registry through registerProjectsJournal.

Projects has its own blocks (capability entries with an inline target), such as a milestone with its progress, tasks and deliverables, a project's progress and the milestones due; each reads Projects live and writes only through the Projects service, so the journal and any page can show and work on projects.
Projects advertises the derived progress of each project, milestone and deliverable as a measurement source, so a goal a project contributes to reads it; an unmeasured project stays unmeasured.
Projects feeds the Sessions due agenda with its live, not completed milestones that have a due date, so the journal agenda and the Global Calendar show them.
Projects serves a read provider for projects and milestones in the shared view registry, so the Tasks aggregated view and the session engine resolve a project parent instead of degrading it.
Projects computes its own metrics for a look-back period (progress change, milestones and deliverables completed); Journals presents them and never recomputes them.

Progress is derived bottom-up on read (task, deliverable, milestone, project); the stored progress is a nullable manual override that wins when set, children weigh by their nesting_weight (empty means equal), an unmeasured child is left out and flags the rollup partial, and an all-unmeasured set is null, never 0. The project to purpose step is weighted by the contribution percentage, not by counting.
A failed rollup or measurement shows a flagged partial or the last-known value, never a wrong progress as truth; a vault read failure is a typed error that never loses or exposes a file.
The data-model record shows the deliverables table, nullable progress, nesting_weight, the retired inline tags and the code-held cascades, and the shared Projects types match the built rows.
Project, milestone and deliverable notes are pages with that entity type, never inline fields.

In the app the composition root builds Projects with its deps (spaces, notes, the entity registry, the measurement sources, the Tasks port and the effect rail); Projects owns no effect handler, so it has no registration step.

A milestone's progress is the weighted rollup, through the measurement engine, of its sub-milestones, its deliverables and each of its own tasks outside a deliverable as one child (equal weight unless set); a task inside a deliverable counts only through that deliverable (Victor, 2026-11-08).
Every milestone has at least one deliverable; creating a milestone takes at least one deliverable, and deleting a milestone's last deliverable is refused (Victor, 2026-11-08).

A deliverable carries measurement_kind (natural milestone) and binding_mode; the five former backends (financial, task statistics, third-party metric, activity log, artifact) become kind by binding by source, a derived-pull deliverable reads its bound source through the measurement-source seam, and the order is manual override, then its tasks, then its source, then unmeasured.

Tasks belong to Tasks; Projects reaches them only through the dedicated Tasks to Projects read port, for the project task list, the task leaf of a deliverable and project time, and never reads the tasks table.
Project time derives from the focus time of the project's tasks (Tasks' one ledger); there is no project timer and no project time log. PJ-15 extends it to sessions attached to the project.
Vision and Mission are guiding pages of the project, not columns; the vision column is a one-line summary at most.

Project documents are a confidential vault, always client-encrypted; small files are stored inline, large files go through the attachment pipeline as ciphertext only, and the server never sees plaintext.

Deleting a project removes its milestones, their deliverables and its documents; deleting a milestone removes its deliverables, moves its sub-milestones to the top level and keeps its documents under the project; a soft delete hides the row and still syncs. What happens to the tasks is PJ-14.
Preferences are plaintext config, never field-encrypted [E]; the repository registers an empty [E] set.

Preferences is the single writer of persona, motivation_style, active_modules and onboarding_* (E9 split off user_profile); personal data and focus_areas stay in user_profile, and no field has two writers.
Notification channels are in_app, push and email, never sms; the per-module push toggles ride the push channel.
Preferences owns the user-managed integration surface (webhooks, external APIs, cookbooks); fetch, egress and connection_config custody stay with the ADR-014 guard, never a preferences column.
Quiet hours are applied when Notifications registers a scheduled alert, and changing a quiet-hours preference reschedules the affected reminders (N7).
Enum preferences reject out-of-set values before persistence (theme, time_format, persona, dock_position, dock_size) through a schema constraint and a typed Zod error.
Module visibility can never hide its own escape hatch; Settings and Home are not hideable, and an unknown module key is a typed InvalidModuleError.
The Settings screen is tabbed and searchable over one settings index, with a calm no-match state, and the Cmd+K palette is a global overlay backed by command_bar_history.
Every Settings pane persists through the preferences seam, Locale and Notifications included.
Each consumer reads its preferences through the seam, never the raw table; Tasks, Pomodoro, Dashboard, the appearance and locale fields and the dock each read theirs.

Onboarding commits only the steps the user continued, as one write through the preferences seam (module visibility seeded from the current visibility, the theme on the shared Settings path, the three non-game presets), and sets onboarding_completed on complete or skip-all, never on Skip for now.
A preference read is never undefined; the stored row, or its absence, is overlaid on the one defaults object, and a malformed map or list field degrades to its default.
The page transition is a preference (page-turn, cross-fade, slide or none) stored as a dashboard_layout sub-key with no schema change, and it reads none while reduce motion is on.
user_preferences and nav_preferences are one row per vault, created on the first write.
Saving is debounced 500 ms and optimistic with no Save button; a failed save reverts the value and shows one typed toast, never a silent drop.
Theme applies app-wide at once; the theme store is a derived cache of the stored row, never a second source.
command_key is unique and recording it again increments use_count; the palette ranks pinned first, then by frecency.
Module visibility (nav show/hide), feature_gamification (whether gamification logic runs) and active_modules are distinct; a module can be hidden yet enabled, or shown yet off.
Settings renders Account/Security and data import/export sections but never stores their data; Auth/Account and Data/Sync own them.
Every preference write succeeds locally first with a co-transactional sync_queue row, and config reconciles Last-Writer-Wins.

A contact's identifying fields (names, nickname, email, phone, avatar, company, job title, location, birthday, how we met, social links) and the free text (an interaction's summary, follow-up notes and key takeaways, an event's title and description, a reminder's title, a group's name and message template, a network's name) are encrypted client-side [E]; the type, sentiment and frequency enums, dates, flags and counts are plaintext config. M1 is a pass-through.
Contact and network tags are shared entity_tags rows written through Spaces, nestable by parent tag, never an inline tag list; the universal versus module tag scope is a Notes and Spaces concern.

Importing phone contacts is device-mediated; the device parses, normalizes and encrypts, the server never sees plaintext and a server-plaintext path is refused, and the merge stages each row against existing contacts (matched, new or a parse error) and commits only on the user's confirmation, never overwriting a contact.
Every create, edit, log and import succeeds locally first, and structured columns sync last-writer-wins.

The user picks the default top view among the Dashboard, the neural Graph and the grouped All-Contacts list; there are contact and network standalone pages, a Reminders page for creating reminders and an All-Events page, while reminders and events are viewed on the Global Calendar; reads and optimistic writes refresh the derived stats and health.

Each Relationships capability renders its terminal states (loading, empty with a call to action, a typed error with retry, populated); a failed save, log or import reverts its optimistic state with a typed error, and a failed health compute shows a flagged partial.
The neural graph view renders the network and contact membership graph with Sigma.js (WebGL), and falls back to the list when the graph fails to build.

Relationships feeds the Sessions due agenda with everything it schedules; besides due reminders, stay-in-touch nudges and group fires, it adds each event's occurrence and its reminder days and each open follow-up date, so the Global Calendar, the journal agenda and Notifications see birthdays and follow-ups.

Relationships has its own blocks (capability entries with an inline target), such as the people to reach out to, the day's events and the reminders due; each reads Relationships live and writes only through the Relationships service, so the journal and any page can show and work on them.

Relationships' journal contribution answers a date with that day's interactions, events and due reminders, empty on an idle day; it is registered into the journal registry through registerRelationshipsJournal.
An event can be edited and deleted and read per contact, and a network can be deleted (its memberships go, its contacts stay), each through the Relationships service.

Deleting a contact removes its events, interactions, reminders and its group and network memberships; a soft delete hides the contact and still syncs, and groups and networks survive. What happens to its tasks is RL-26.
A schedule group at every frequency fires on time; biweekly, monthly, quarterly and yearly groups have a phase anchor, so the due agenda projects them like daily and weekly groups.
An event (a birthday's present) or an interaction's follow-up can create a Task linked to the contact through the Tasks service; the event never becomes the task.
Relationships reads the user's reminder defaults, closeness tier definitions and import settings from Preferences, never its own store.
Interaction streaks feed Gamification, which owns the rule and the reward; Relationships adds no economy contract.
A contact's due-time reminders are gated by the Preferences push_contacts toggle.
Relationships serves a read provider for contacts in the shared view registry, so the Tasks aggregated view and the session engine resolve a contact parent instead of degrading it.

Deleting a contact asks the user what happens to its tasks (delete, unlink or move them) and calls the Tasks operations for the choice before the cascade; Relationships never leaves a task pointing at a deleted contact.
A contact page lists the contact's tasks through the Tasks service by its contact link, never a table read.
Other modules link a contact (a project's contacts with roles) through the Relationships contact read, and deleting a contact never leaves those links pointing at it.

In the app the composition root builds Relationships with its deps (spaces, notes) and registers its due lane; once they exist it also passes tasks (RL-21) and a Preferences port (RL-22), and registers the contact read provider (RL-25) and the journal contribution (RL-18). Relationships owns no effect handler and emits nothing, so it has no effects dep or registration step.

A contact's last interaction date and interaction count recompute from the interactions ledger on every interaction change, and its next contact date is the last interaction plus the stay-in-touch cadence (exact days override the frequency); the columns are a cache and the ledger is the truth.

The data-model record shows the eight Relationships tables (networks and their junction included), the closeness tier, how we met, the interaction energy and key takeaways, reminder snooze and priority, the group birthday anchor, the retired inline tags and the code-held cascades.

Relationship type, interaction type, sentiment, event type and frequency are closed enums declared once (string unions, `CHECK` constraints and `Zod` schemas); closeness tier is open vocabulary; an event date is `MM-DD` or `YYYY-MM-DD`.
Contact and network descriptions are pages with that entity type, only an interaction's short summary stays inline, and a contact is a valid entity link target.
A contact may belong to many networks through the membership junction; the neural graph links each contact node to its network nodes and draws no contact to contact edges.

Relationship health is derived on read and never stored; it comes from the time since the last interaction against the cadence and the recent sentiment, weighted by closeness (inner tiers penalize neglect more), banded Healthy, At-risk or Overdue, new for a contact with no interactions, and a network's health aggregates its members. It is a derived analytic, never an ADR-011 pursuable or a measurement source.

Three reminder mechanisms each produce notifications through the Sessions due agenda; the stay-in-touch cadence gives an overdue-to-reach-out nudge, an explicit contact reminder fires one-off or recurring, and a reminder group nudges for its members; Notifications dispatches and Relationships only produces.

A reminder group's message template reminds the user and never sends anything; no contact data leaves in an off-device push (the device composes the nudge after decrypting); a group can fire relative to each member's birthday, and can target the user's important people by closeness.
A contact event is time-anchored (a year-agnostic `MM-DD` date recurs yearly) and never completes; creating a task or a nudge from it is RL-21 and RL-16.
An interaction can flag a follow-up with a date; the actual to-do is a Task linked by its contact link and owned by Tasks. Surfacing the follow-up date is RL-16, and creating the task is RL-21.

A routine's name and description, a step's title and description and a completion's skip_reason are encrypted client-side [E]; lifecycle, the recurrence rule, step type and order, time_of_day, skip_dates and dates are plaintext config. M1 is a pass-through.
One repeatable step may be scoped to all routines, one routine or a subset, one action with many routine memberships.

A routine's cadence is broad (a day, a weekday, a day of the month, a day of the year, at day grain) and validated at write; its occurrences reach the Calendar and the agenda through the Sessions due agenda, with no Routines-owned scheduler.

Routines pushes nothing to Purposes; a purpose, goal or dream a routine relates to reads the routine's days through the Routines service and computes them into that day's progress, and only the up-edge to the purpose is weighted.
Routines is a due provider; it serves its scheduled, still-owed occurrences through dueIn as one Sessions due lane, read live by the Calendar and the agenda, with nothing mirrored.

Streaks, completion rate, step ranking and period comparison recompute from routine_completions on every read; Routines keeps no cached counters, and editing or deleting a past completion re-derives them.
Notes attach to a routine and to a step through a linked note page, never inline.
Routines and steps are tagged through the shared entity_tags primitive that Spaces owns, as a consumer, never a Routines tag store.
Deleting a step deletes its completions and deleting a routine deletes its steps; a soft delete (archive) hides them and keeps the ledger.
Every create, edit, complete, skip and reschedule succeeds locally first with a co-transactional sync_queue row; structured columns reconcile Last-Writer-Wins, and the ledger merges by step and date.

A routine is a pursuable with measurement_kind (natural rate) and binding_mode (derived-pull); it has no goal-type column, progress derives on read with a nullable 0 to 100 override, and it is not a measurement source.
A routine is a named, ordered sequence that owns its list of steps, not a loose time-of-day bucket of single actions.

The user's routine policy (the completion kind and its params, how a logged skip counts, the acceptance window) is stored once outside Routines and served through the Routines policy port, with editable shipped presets; Routines hardcodes none and flags a routine with no policy (RT-5 and RT-6's store half).
Steps may be done in any order, unless the user's policy marks a step as a prerequisite, which gates the steps after it.
Rescheduling a missed occurrence writes one intent block for it, and the scheduling engine places that block in an open slot that fits (RT-4's reschedule half).

A done routine-day grants experience points through `award_xp`, applied by Gamification as `grant_currency(XP)` into the consequence_ledger, once per routine and date; Routines never writes points (RT-7's economy half).
The journal's daily summary pulls each routine with activity on the day, its steps done and skipped and its evaluation, through the Routines journal contribution (RT-13's summary half).
Routines presets its recurring windows into the Planner's availability, so the scheduling engine plans around them (the Routines side of SS-9).

In the app the routines service is composed with Tasks, Sessions and its sub-type registry, Habits, the policy port, the shared effect rail and registry, Spaces and Notes; Routines owns no effect handler of its own.
Routines serves a routine_step read provider on the shared view-provider registry, so Sessions shows a step's title and detects a deleted step.
A routine's due-time reminders are gated by the Preferences push_routines toggle.

Routines has its cockpit surfaces, today's routines grouped by time of day with each step's live entity state, running a step in place, and the per-routine page (streak, trend, calendar, step ranking, period comparison), plus the policy settings.

A step references the entity it drives by type and ref, and running it drives that entity, through a session sub-type or the entity's own completion; the routine reflects the entity and stamps only its own occurrence row, never a parallel completion or a second effect.

Every Routines surface renders its terminal states (today's list, running a step, the alarm step, the routine's evaluation, skip and reschedule, the per-routine page, the provider read); a failed write leaves the step open and shows a typed error.
The user extends the step and session types and saves routine views through Spaces; Routines never invents a step mode where a session sub-type exists.

A failed purpose contribution, effect or provider read never fails the routine; the write is flagged, the contribution can be re-driven, and one routine's failure leaves the other routines unaffected.
A driven entity that is missing, terminal or not drivable gives the step a typed error before any routine write; the step stays open and is never marked done silently.
An actionable step with no rich entity is a Task that recurs within a timeframe, alarm-like; checked inside the timeframe it is done, missed it is not done.

At the timeframe's end the routine computes what was done and what was not; that partial record is always kept and shown positively, and whether the routine counts as done is the user's completion policy (all-or-nothing, a required step, or a threshold).

The user sets how misses count and the acceptance window, how long a miss stays make-good-able before it is a real miss, and a make-good past the window is refused with a typed error; a routine is active, paused or off, and a paused or off routine generates no misses.
A routine streak is derived from the routine's own completion and miss policy, not a fixed rule; Gamification reads that policy-derived streak and never assumes the Habits rule.
A pre-planned skip (the step's skip_dates) and a skip logged on the day (a completion row with its reason) are distinct; a planned skip is neutral, and a logged skip counts as the miss policy says.
A habit is one tracked behavior and a routine the orchestrator that sequences steps; they never merge, and a habit step drives its habit without redefining it.
Study methods are the study_method partition of the one capability registry, never a parallel store.

Curves schedule as designed; the shipped `SM-2` preset and the decay, review and test curves set each next interval from the review's quality and history under the user's parameters, never a fixed one-day fallback.
When a kind has no default method, its learning realm picks one from the methods that declare that realm, memorize toward drills and understand toward elaboration.

Each object takes the nearest binding above it on the spine, mixable per level, so a bound topic or kind schedules the objects under it; the due queue reports objects, never the bound level itself, and honors each binding's daily cap.
Leaf mastery derives from every active method's review events under the object's bound curve (weighting and decay), not only the latest quality.
The review engine schedules reviewables only; Journals' look-back, Purposes' target and purpose reviews and Check-ins' review check-ins are separate things, never engine reviews.
A study method declares an empty privilege envelope (no render targets, effects, bindings or terminal states), and its roles and configuration ride its config schema.
Review curves are user-defined and personalizable, and `SM-2` is one preset among them.
A binding ties a method and an optional curve to any spine level (area, subject, unit, topic or kind); its method and curve references aren't checked, so a method not yet registered can be bound.
The default method resolves from the kind's own default and otherwise none; the engine never invents a method id.
Curves and bindings soft-delete and every read filters deleted rows, and removing a missing curve or binding is a typed error.
Recording a review appends an immutable review event and never writes mastery.
The engine is the due-queue provider; a bound target is due once its interval has passed since its last review, and a bound target never reviewed is due now.
Leaf mastery is derived on read, 0 to 100, or null when nothing measured it; a quality of 0 reads 0, and the engine never reads a stored mastery.

A skill is a goal-driven capability in exactly one life domain (health, career, finance, relationships, personal growth, spiritual, recreation, environment), with why it matters and the mastery and date it targets.
Target mastery is a Purposes target, the pursuable that carries the measurement kind and binding mode; Purposes reads a skill's mastery live through Skills and keeps no copy.

Evidence (a project, a recording, a certificate) proves mastery through pages, attachments and project activities, and a dev-log's key insights become Knowledge objects, created through Knowledge's service, in the user's principles store.

Skills' names and free text (a skill's name, description and why it matters, a level's criteria, indicators, challenges and key skills, an activity's instructions, prerequisites and success criteria, a dev-log's reflections and insights, a definition's name, templates and provenance, the measurement config) are encrypted client-side; enums, dates, ratings and counters stay plaintext.
Skills composes Sessions, Knowledge, Projects, Purposes, Spaces and Health's adaptation engine and adds only the capability spine, the Composer and the graph, never parallel machinery.

The skill library import is a device-mediated public-reference whole-set fetch under the external-in grant, add-only, revocable and normalized per source, and the server never proxies it; a model draft is a scoped generate on the device or in the cloud as egress, never an agent, imported content carries its provenance into any prompt, and generated rows carry the ai source.

Skills' entity types (skill, level, activity, dev-log, dependency, definition) register in the open taggable-type registry, so tags, notes and links reach them, and entity links replace the retired course-and-book resource junction; Skills owns no tag table.

A dev-log is the reflection on a practice session (how it felt, what worked, what to improve, the next plan, key insights) through the adaptation engine Skills shares with Health, so a skill can run experiments on the user's own learning; it reads the session's date and length instead of storing them.

Skills builds on other modules' entities instead of copying them; practice is a session of the practice sub_type, an assessment is a task of a Skills type, a study activity is a Knowledge study session and a project activity a Projects project, each anchored to its skill and level and tracked Skills' way with what the base lacks, and habits, routines and the other modules attach and link to Skills entities.

The user prepares inside Skills following its hierarchy; preparation (the practice cadence, reminders, and sessions scheduled automatically before a level's target or the target mastery date) is set on a skill and passed down to its levels, activities and the sessions, tasks, projects and reviews they create, and any entity below can override it; Sessions generates the sessions as planned blocks next to the other modules' entities.

Skills runs no due lane of its own; its due items ride their base entities, so practice is due as a planned session, an assessment as a task and decay maintenance as a review on Knowledge's lane, and they reach Today, the Calendar and reminders like any session, task or review.

Each skill defines its own ladder as data, ordered levels with completion criteria and success indicators, never one universal scale; ladder templates (belts, ranks, milestones, language levels) seed a ladder.

Skills ships the practice sub_type fully configured and registers it with Sessions; every practice is a session the user can name and type, attached to its activity, so the agenda and a routine step drive it.

Skills exposes its skills, levels and activities and their events (a level reached, a practice done or missed, a skill at risk of decay) and measures (level, progress, mastery, practice consistency) as measurement sources and rule subjects that Purposes and Gamification read live; nothing copies Skills' data.
A level-up, a mastery reached and a practice streak emit the grant-currency feeder that Gamification applies; Skills emits the signal and never writes points.
Skills contributes its day to the journal (practice done, levels reached, skills at risk), read live through its contribution.

Skills has its own journal blocks and capability blocks, the life skill tree over the graph among them; each reads Skills live and writes only through Skills' service, separate from its journal contribution.
Skills serves a read provider for its entity types, so links, views, the graph and search resolve a skill, level, activity, dev-log or definition through Skills.
When the root composes Skills, Skills registers its practice sub_type and task types, its measurement sources, its journal contribution and its read provider; nothing is wired centrally.

The global skill library and its graph, the locale variants of its definitions, ladder templates, activity templates and curated resources ship as opt-in default datasets the user accepts or declines, refreshed as a whole set and read from a local copy; the pattern is built even when declined.

The data model's record shows the Skills tables migration 021 built (seven tables, no foreign keys, the practice extension excluded from the entity types and without deleted_at, the resource junction retired, the older stored mastery default resolved out).

Skills' surfaces show every capability's terminal states (a skill planning, active, maintaining or completed, a Composer setup quick, advanced or incomplete, a fill by hand, drafting, failed or importing, a level upcoming, active or complete, a practice planned, in progress, complete or skipped, mastery with too little data, derived or overridden, a graph with no edges, a recommended path or a synergy, a decay flag none, at risk or dismissed).

A skill's definition, ladder and activities fill by hand, by an opt-in model call or by import from the curated skill library; definitions vary by locale (language, region, culture) and dedupe by name and locale, a miss falls back to manual, a model draft or a community template import, and Vida never submits to a community, the user's generic template export being the only bridge.

Mastery derives on read from gates, activities, assessments, linked Knowledge mastery and practice consistency, and a manual override is flagged; an ability that can't be measured digitally is qualitative, self-rated or evidence-based, and Vida never fakes a number.

The Skill Composer defines each skill, what it is, which modules it works with, what's tracked and how progress and mastery are measured (a measurement kind with derived-pull binding, referenced and never stored as a pursuable column), in a quick mode from a template or an advanced custom mode.

An activity's type sends its work to the owning module and anchors the entity there to its level; practice is a session, study a Knowledge study session on the skill's compound set, a project a Projects project, an assessment a task of a Skills type linked to Knowledge, and a review the review engine; Skills orchestrates like Routines.
A practice action is a session of the practice sub_type with Skills' one-to-one extension, the base session owning time and lifecycle, and practice time derives from the sessions.

The skill graph links skills by requires, unlocks and synergy edges, in a global canonical graph with shared foundational skills and the user's personal instance; it recommends a path and detects synergies between goals, and the global graph grows by model drafts, curated additions, the user and community imports.
An unpracticed skill decays through the review engine's curve, and its maintenance due item and reminder are advisory, configurable per skill and never nagging.
A session is exactly one sub_type over one shared spine; pomodoro is the focus runtime, never a sub_type, and each owning module registers its own sub_type.
On completion the engine emits a signal (duration, resource, outcome); Knowledge owns mastery and Education owns pace, and Sessions never computes a domain measure.
Pomodoro is the focus sub_type's runtime, owned in the Sessions realm and keyed by session_id; the Notes /pomodoro block is a lens onto focus sessions, never the owner.
Session analytics (completion rate, average focus, planned-vs-actual, time per module, streaks) are derived on read from the session log, never stored in synced aggregate tables.
A dueIn provider lane that fails degrades only that lane with a typed ProviderUnavailable(module), the other lanes render, and the engine never writes another module's schedule to recover.

generatePlan(scope, window) plans across every module, not one course, and a batch travels draft, pending_approval, approved, active, then completed or failed; no availability or nothing to schedule fails explicitly (NoAvailability, NothingToSchedule), never as an empty batch.
A planned block whose target due work vanished before it ran resolves to empty and is dropped or flagged, never left as a dangling row.
A session with ended_at before started_at, or a duration beyond its block window, is a typed validation error and is never stored.
Editing a shipped type is allowed behind a not-recommended warning, scoped to the user's device and never pushed as a default.
Sessions has its own view family (Hub, wizard, Management, Availability, per-type tools) and an empty state that offers a starter availability grid and the shipped types.
An effect whose attached entity was deleted no-ops loudly with a typed AttachmentTargetMissing; it never resurrects the entity or fails the whole completion.
sub_type (the tool family and owner) and purpose (why) are separate axes and separate enums, never one conflated enum.

Every completion goes through one door, transition(), which checks that every declared non-projection effect has a handler before any write (NoEffectHandler), treats a soft-deleted session as missing, and counts as fired only the effects the ledger applied.
Whether a completed session's effects were applied is derived on read from the applied_effects ledger, never stored as a flag, and a replay re-applies only the effects with no ledger row.
Sessions ships the study sub_type, fully configured in all four dimensions, as the scheduling engine's own generated sessions; focus and study are the shipped roster.
No session type, shipped or user-made, exists without all four Integration Contract dimensions declared (attachment, effects, lifecycle, permissions).
Every identified sub_type ships fully configured by us; the user never sets up the main ones, and user extensibility is for new long-tail types only.
A user-created type may attach to any entity and declare effects only inside its permission envelope, and sensitive-module effects (Finance, Health) need explicit opt-in consent.

A session never affects an entity it is not attached to, two types never count the same event twice (deterministic effect_event_id over the applied_effects ledger), and a permission violation is a hard, logged rejection.
The engine owns planned_blocks and its own generated sessions but never stores a copy of another module's due work; the agenda is its own blocks plus live dueIn provider reads.
A planned_block is the plan and never the log; completing it calls the owner's createSession(), which carries planned_block_id.
Availability windows and exceptions are Planner-owned scheduling input; Routines may preset recurring windows, and attended sessions consume availability while planned ones fill it.
A task's title, description and tag associations are encrypted client-side [E]; status, priority, difficulty, dates and estimates are plaintext config. M1 is a pass-through.
Every create, edit, complete and timer action succeeds locally first with a co-transactional sync_queue row, and structured columns reconcile Last-Writer-Wins across devices.

A task is a pursuable with measurement_kind (natural milestone) and binding_mode (completion is the event trigger); it stores no progress column, is never an M5 measure source, and contributes up to a purpose only through contributions.

Deleting a parent module's entity (project, milestone, course or contact) asks the user what happens to its tasks, deleting them with it, unlinking them into standalone tasks, or moving them to another entity, either nested inside it (a milestone) or at its top level; tasks are never deleted silently.
A project, course or contact page lists its tasks through the Tasks service by its parent link, never a table read; Tasks serves the read port Projects declares (listProjectTasks, getFocusMinutes).

A focus run bound to a task writes its real minutes into the task's one ledger through attach_pomodoro and log_time, the same ledger the work timer writes (TK-5's deferred task_time_logs and session reconciliation).

Completing a task grants experience points through `award_xp`, applied by Gamification as `grant_currency(XP)` into the consequence_ledger; one task grants once, ever, each obligation occurrence grants anew, and Tasks never writes points itself.

A task's completion emits emit_measurement_signal for the measurement engine and pushes nothing to Purposes; a purpose, goal or dream a task relates to reads it through the Tasks service and computes it into that day's progress.
The journal's daily summary pulls the tasks completed, due or scheduled on the day through the Tasks journal contribution; Tasks never pushes surface_journal.
A task's scheduled_date is the planned work date, distinct from due_date; both feed Today, the Calendar and the Sessions due-work lane, with the deadline carried as hard_deadline.

The All-Tasks screen hosts the base task layouts as selectable renderers over one saved-view config, with a view-builder that saves named views rows (filter, layout, grouping), global or Space-owned, and offers a preset when no custom view exists.

A task sets at most one of project_id, milestone_id, course_id and contact_id, and a milestone implies its project; two parent FKs are a typed MultipleParentError, and a task with none is a first-class standalone task.
The twelve task layouts map onto the seven ADR-007 view layouts as layout, filter and grouping configs, and no task_views table exists.
A task preset is a saved views config plus per-type defaults, bound to the task kind discriminator (standard or obligation); the preset never owns a discriminator of its own.
The user pins and reorders saved task views per Space, stored by Preferences as per-view nav placement and read by the Tasks view switcher.
The task detail shows the task's fields, its sub-tasks with the rollup, its time logs and timer, its linked note and its focus runs; a sub-task is created only through addSubtask.

Every Tasks surface renders its terminal states (task list or view, create and edit, sub-task rollup, timer, obligation completion, view-builder); a failed save or timer action reverts and shows a typed error, and an obligation that can't regenerate completes and is flagged.

React Query owns task reads and writes, with optimistic create, edit and complete that show at once and revert on failure, and paginated lists for large sets; Zustand owns the ephemeral screen state (active view, view-builder draft, running timer, board drag, selection). The /tasks route's invalidate-and-reread is replaced.

Tasks has its own block, the task checklist, an inline capability entry; it lists tasks filtered by project, milestone, deliverable or due date with its terminal states, reads Tasks live, and ticks, unticks and creates tasks only through the Tasks service; on a journal page it shows that day's tasks through the Tasks journal contribution.

Sub-tasks are one level; the parent shows the ADR-011 M4 weighted rollup of its children (per-child nesting weight, equal by default), derived on read with no stored progress, and completing a parent never completes its children, nor the reverse.
Deleting a task deletes its sub-tasks and its task_time_logs.

Time is one ledger; actual_minutes is the sum of the task's task_time_logs, written only by the log_time effect of the work session the timer opens, never a direct client write, and a task may opt out of time tracking (no logs, no rollup).

A task is complete when status is completed and completed_at is set, and reopening clears it; the completion is the task's event trigger and fires the S4 effects through the rail, idempotently, so in the app the tasks service is composed with the effect rail.

Only an obligation recurs; completing an obligation with a recurrence rule spawns exactly one next occurrence with the next due_date, even after a reopen and re-complete, and standard tasks never recur.
Tasks tag through the shared entity_tags primitive with entity_type task, never a private inline tag list.

The aggregated view reads only the tasks table and resolves parent-module data through the R7 read seam (the shared ViewProviderRegistry); a source that is down degrades only its own group, and standalone tasks form the Inbox group.
